MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning

Jiangcheng Song Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: enone@stu.xjtu.edu.cn    Haodong Jing Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: nnzheng@xjtu.edu.cn    Yulin Mu Affiliation: Faculty of Electronic and Information EngineeringXi’an Jiaotong University    Lesong Tao Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University    Jixin Wang Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University    Jin Cui Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University    Tianjing Ren Affiliation: Imperial College London    Runxuan Xie Affiliation: Faculty of Electronic and Information EngineeringXi’an Jiaotong University    Yongqiang Ma Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University    Nanning Zheng ††thanks: Corresponding author: nnzheng@xjtu.edu.cn. Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented IntelligenceInstitute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics,Xi’an Jiaotong University
Abstract

Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman’s account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet11 1 Project page: jiangchengsong.github.io/MemDuet/., a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74×\times and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.

1 Introduction

Long-context reasoning is essential for large language models (LLMs) to synthesize evidence across documents, understand lengthy reports, and resolve repository-level dependencies in code (Bai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023). Existing work primarily extends long-context capability through larger context windows, sparse or linear attention, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Chen et al., 2023b; Beltagy et al., 2020; Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2025; Lewis et al., 2020). However, these approaches remain bounded by the amount of context that can be directly represented or retrieved, leaving reasoning over unbounded documents unresolved.

MemAgent instead streams documents through a bounded recurrent memory, enabling reasoning over infinitely long documents with a fixed active context (Yu et al., 2026). Building on this paradigm, InfMem and GRU-Mem learn when to retrieve, update, or stop, while LycheeMemory compresses each chunk and invokes the reasoner only for selected memory blocks (Wang et al., 2026; Sheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). These advances make recurrent memory increasingly selective, but expose a common bottleneck: control decisions either remain inside the sequential recurrent loop or operate on representations in which the original evidence has already been compressed. Consequently, as context grows, reasoning performance and inference efficiency remain tightly coupled.

Human reading and memory suggest a different principle: memory formation begins with selective attention. Readers first focus on goal-relevant information and then integrate the attended evidence with prior knowledge into a coherent memory representation (Craik et al., 1996; Kintsch, 1988; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016). This process naturally maps onto the dual-process account of cognition: System 1 rapidly identifies potentially useful evidence, whereas System 2 deliberately assesses and consolidates it (Kahneman, 2011; Evans and Stanovich, 2013). Based on this insight, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process recurrent memory framework. A small language model (System 1) scans raw context in parallel to select candidate chunks for memory updating. A large language model (System 2) verifies whether each selected chunk warrants a memory update under the current memory, then rewrites memory. By combining small-model selective attention over raw chunks with large-model verification and memory updating, MemDuet balances reasoning performance and inference efficiency as context grows.

A key challenge is how to train the two systems to cooperate. We develop a progressive three-stage training strategy. First, we supervise System 1 to identify context chunks that are likely to trigger useful memory updates. Next, with System 1 fixed, we optimize System 2 using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024), training it to verify memory-update decisions and rewrite memory toward successful downstream reasoning. Finally, we jointly optimize both systems with task-level rewards, allowing evidence selection and memory updating to co-adapt.

We evaluate MemDuet on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and long-context 2WikiMultihopQA. Results show that MemDuet improves the performance–efficiency trade-off over full-update recurrent memory agents, scaling to 3.5M-token contexts while achieving higher reasoning accuracy with substantially lower inference cost.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We propose MemDuet, a cognitively inspired dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning, which instantiates System 1 as fast, parallel evidence selection with a small language model and System 2 as memory-update verification and memory rewriting with a large language model.

  2. 2.

    We develop a three-stage training strategy that first establishes the selection and memory-updating capabilities of the two systems through SFT and GRPO, respectively, and then jointly optimizes their cooperation under a shared downstream reasoning objective.

  3. 3.

    Extensive experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MemDuet achieves a favorable balance between reasoning performance and inference efficiency.

2 Related Work

2.1 Recurrent Memory for Long-Context Reasoning

Recurrent-memory methods process documents incrementally while maintaining a bounded state, allowing language models to handle inputs far beyond their context windows. MemAgent sequentially processes text chunks and repeatedly rewrites a textual memory, using end-to-end reinforcement learning to retain task-relevant information and discard distractors based on downstream rewards (Yu et al., 2026). Building on this paradigm, InfMem and GRU-Mem learn retrieval, memory updating, and early-stopping decisions through SFT-to-RL training or behavior-specific rewards (Wang et al., 2026; Sheng et al., 2026). LycheeMemory compresses individual chunks and selectively invokes the reasoner, jointly optimizing its compressor and reasoner through end-to-end reinforcement learning (Chen et al., 2026). These studies turn memory management from a fixed procedure into a task-driven policy, but their control decisions remain within the sequential loop or operate on already compressed evidence. MemDuet instead scans raw chunks in parallel before recurrent updating and progressively coordinates evidence selection with memory consolidation.

2.2 Cognitively Inspired Language Models and Memory

Cognitive theories have informed both memory design and computational allocation in language-model systems. CoALA organizes language agents around modular memory, decision-making, and action components derived from cognitive architectures (Sumers et al., 2024). MemoryBank adopts an Ebbinghaus-inspired mechanism for dynamically forgetting and reinforcing memories (Zhong et al., 2024), whereas HippoRAG draws on hippocampal indexing theory to support associative knowledge retrieval (Gutiérrez et al., 2024). For reasoning, System 2 Attention deliberately rewrites the context to remove irrelevant information (Weston and Sukhbaatar, 2023), while Dualformer learns switchable fast and slow reasoning modes within a single model (Su et al., 2025). These studies primarily apply cognitive principles to memory organization, retrieval, or the allocation of reasoning effort. MemDuet instead introduces dual-process specialization into recurrent memory: System 1 selects raw candidate chunks in parallel; System 2 verifies whether they warrant memory updates under the current memory and consolidates their evidence.

3 Methodology

3.1 Preliminaries

Problem setup.

We consider query-conditioned reasoning over a long document DD. Given a query qq, the goal is to generate an answer yy using evidence from DD, whose length may exceed the model’s context window. We divide DD into TT chunks (c1,…,cT)(c_{1},\ldots,c_{T}) in their original order, with |ci|≤C|c_{i}|\leq C, where |⋅||\cdot| denotes token length and CC is the chunk-size budget. The query is available throughout document processing.

Recurrent textual memory.

Following MemAgent (Yu et al., 2026), an LLM carries information across chunks through bounded textual memory, using the common interface

m′∼πθmem(⋅∣q,ci,m),|m′|≤B,m^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}}(\cdot\mid q,c_{i},m),\qquad|m^{\prime}|\leq B, (1)

Here mm and m′m^{\prime} are the preceding and replacement memories, and BB is the memory budget. Under the memory prompt, πθmem\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}} is the autoregressive product of System 2’s next-token policy πθgen\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{gen}}. The same model answers from qq and the final memory under the answer prompt. Both CC and BB are independent of document length.

3.2 MemDuet Workflow

MemDuet alternates parallel raw-chunk selection by System 1 with verification and memory updates in document order by System 2 (Figure 2).

3.2.1 System 1: Memory-Conditioned Parallel Candidate Selection

Here tt indexes speculative rounds and ii document chunks. At round tt, System 1 independently evaluates a window 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t} of up to kk consecutive chunks in parallel, using the shared query qq and memory mtm_{t} to select candidate chunks for memory updating:

at,i\displaystyle a_{t,i} ∼πϕsel(⋅∣q,ci,mt),\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{sel}}\left(\cdot\mid q,c_{i},m_{t}\right), (2)
at,i\displaystyle a_{t,i} ∈{Skip,Update}.\displaystyle\in\{\text{Skip}{},\text{Update}{}\}.

The chunks predicted as Update form the candidate set

𝒞t={ci∈𝒲t∣at,i=Update},\mathcal{C}_{t}=\{c_{i}\in\mathcal{W}_{t}\mid a_{t,i}=\text{Update}{}\}, (3)

which is forwarded to System 2.

3.2.2 System 2: Speculative Verification and Memory Consolidation

Inspired by speculative decoding’s acceptance rule (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a), System 2’s binary policy πθver\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ver}} assesses whether selected chunks warrant memory updates. For candidate indices ℐt={i∣ci∈𝒞t}\mathcal{I}_{t}=\{i\mid c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\}, the action-level acceptance probability is

αt,i=min⁡(1,πθver​(Update∣q,ci,mt)πϕsel​(Update∣q,ci,mt)).\alpha_{t,i}=\min\!\left(1,\,\frac{\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ver}}(\text{Update}{}\mid q,c_{i},m_{t})}{\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{sel}}(\text{Update}{}\mid q,c_{i},m_{t})}\right). (4)

Independently draw ξt,i∼𝒰⁡(0,1)\xi_{t,i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) for each candidate and accept it if ξt,i≤αt,i\xi_{t,i}\leq\alpha_{t,i}.

If any candidate is accepted, commit the first accepted chunk in document order and generate its replacement memory:

mt+1∼πθmem(⋅∣q,cit⋆,mt),m_{t+1}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}}(\cdot\mid q,c_{i_{t}^{\star}},m_{t}), (5)

where it⋆=min⁡{i∈ℐt∣ξt,i≤αt,i}i_{t}^{\star}=\min\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\mid\xi_{t,i}\leq\alpha_{t,i}\}. As a special case, if no candidate is accepted, retain the current memory and advance past the window. Otherwise, discard remaining predictions conditioned on mtm_{t} and resume immediately after the committed chunk with mt+1m_{t+1}. Answering uses the query and final memory; Algorithm B.4 in Appendix B.4 gives the complete transitions.

3.3 Training of MemDuet

Figure 3 summarizes three-stage training. Stage I trains memory-conditioned evidence selection. Stage II freezes System 1 and trains System 2 to verify candidates, rewrite memory, and generate answers. Stage III jointly optimizes both systems with task rewards, coordinating selection with verification and memory updates.

3.3.1 Stage I: System 1 Supervised Warm-up

We initialize System 1 on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) by aligning gold supporting facts with document chunks. Evidence-containing chunks are labeled Update, and other chunks Skip.

For each Update example (q,c,m)(q,c,m), let m′m^{\prime} be the memory after incorporating the evidence from cc. We retain the original example and add a post-update negative:

(q,c,m)\displaystyle(q,c,m) ⟶Update,\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Update}{}, (6)
(q,c,m′)\displaystyle(q,c,m^{\prime}) ⟶Skip.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Skip}{}.

We train on the original examples and post-update negatives using the memory-contrastive objective:

ℒStage​I​(ϕ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Stage\,I}}(\phi)={} ℒwCE+λpair​ℒpair,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wCE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pair}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}, (7)

Here, ℒwCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wCE}} is class-weighted action cross-entropy; 𝒫\mathcal{P} contains matched memory pairs, with Δ​sϕ=sϕ​(q,c,m)−sϕ​(q,c,m′)\Delta s_{\phi}=s_{\phi}(q,c,m)-s_{\phi}(q,c,m^{\prime}). The score sϕs_{\phi} is the UPDATE-minus-SKIP logit difference, and γ\gamma is the margin. Hyperparameters are reported in Appendix B.1.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and evaluation.

We follow MemAgent’s RULER-HQA construction (7K–3.5M tokens) (Yu et al., 2026), reserving its 128-question development set for testing and a disjoint 128-question HotpotQA validation set for checkpoint selection. We further evaluate on LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) and a long-context variant of 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020). We report option accuracy on LongBench v2 and normalized substring exact match (sub-EM) on RULER-HQA and 2WikiMultihopQA. To assess inference efficiency, we additionally report speedup relative to MemAgent and the number of generated output tokens. Dataset construction, sample sizes, and length groupings are detailed in Appendix A.1; evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A.3.

Baselines.

We compare MemDuet with Search-R1-7B (Jin et al., 2025a), QwenLong-L1-32B (Wan et al., 2025), DS-Distill-32B (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), RL-MemAgent-7B (Yu et al., 2026), LycheeMemory-7B (Chen et al., 2026), and ReMemR1-7B (Shi et al., 2025).

Implementation.

We use Qwen3.5-2B as System 1 for the main results and evaluate Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen3.5-0.8B in the System 1 backbone comparison (Yang et al., 2025a; Qwen Team, 2026). System 2 uses the same Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone as MemAgent (Yang et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2026). See Appendix B for training and implementation.

4.2 Main Results

Length scaling on RULER-HQA.

Table 1 shows that MemDuet achieves an increasingly favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off as context grows. At 3.5M tokens, it outperforms RL-MemAgent by 3.90 points while achieving a 49.61×\times speedup and generating 99.14% fewer output tokens. At 7K, the limited number of chunks provides little opportunity to offset the fixed cost of System 1 scanning and cross-system coordination. As the context grows, this overhead is amortized and more unnecessary System 2 processing can be avoided, making the efficiency gains increasingly pronounced without sacrificing accuracy.

Generalization to realistic long-context tasks.

Table 2 evaluates MemDuet on LongBench v2, which contains realistic long-context tasks, and on length-controlled 2WikiMultihopQA. MemDuet achieves the highest option accuracy on the Long and Ultra groups of LongBench v2, with 3.00×\times and 8.03×\times speedups. Its lower option accuracy on the Short and Medium groups is consistent with selective processing occasionally discarding useful evidence when the full input is still manageable. The same transition appears in sub-EM on 2WikiMultihopQA: MemDuet trails at 14K and 56K, but leads at 224K and 896K, indicating that its advantages are concentrated in the long-context regime for which it is designed.

4.3 Analysis

Efficiency scaling.

Figure 4 shows that MemDuet’s latency and output tokens grow more slowly with context length than those of RL-MemAgent. Although MemDuet incurs a small latency overhead at 7K, its runtime advantage becomes increasingly pronounced on longer inputs. The shallower growth in output tokens is consistent with restricting large-model memory updates to selected evidence rather than rewriting memory for every chunk. Latency savings are smaller than token savings, since input processing and System 1 computation remain necessary even when output tokens are substantially reduced.

Inference mechanisms.

W/o draft–verify retains System 1 selection but removes System 2 verification and acceptance tests: selected Update actions directly trigger memory rewriting, followed by reevaluation of later chunks. W/o state reevaluation reuses selection and verification/acceptance results computed with the window-start memory even after updates, processing chunks in document order; memory generation still uses the latest memory. W/o parallel execution changes k=4k=4 to k=1k=1, retaining all other decision rules. The k=1k=1 variant preserves accuracy, with speedup changing from 12.16×12.16\times to 11.84×11.84\times. Removing draft–verify or state reevaluation reduces accuracy by up to 3.90 points; draft–verify removal also lowers speedup to 9.89×9.89\times. Verification and state reevaluation thus preserve quality while reducing large-model computation.

Three-stage training.

The three training stages play complementary roles. Without Stage I, System 1 tends to propose updates for nearly all chunks, maintaining coverage of supporting evidence and limiting the accuracy drop to 3.90–5.47 points relative to the full configuration. More frequent verification and memory rewriting increase computation, reducing speedup from 12.16×12.16\times to 2.54×2.54\times and roughly tripling the mean output-token ratio. Without Stage II, System 2 lacks dedicated reinforcement learning for memory rewriting, substantially weakening evidence consolidation. The retained Stage III joint training partially restores this capability, keeping accuracy above the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline (112K: 32.81%; 448K: 6.25%; 896K: 1.56%). Stage III aligns the two policies: joint optimization recovers 2.34–6.25 accuracy points over w/o Stage III. The curriculum thus progressively learns when to update, how to update, and how to coordinate the two decisions.

Choice of System 1.

System 1 should favor evidence coverage, since missed evidence cannot be recovered, whereas false positives can still be filtered by System 2. Across both Qwen2.5 and Qwen3.5 backbones, MemDuet consistently turns small models into effective proposers, achieving 80.08–83.36% downstream accuracy with mean speedups of 5.695.69–14.26×14.26\times. Qwen3.5-0.8B has the highest selection F1 and lowest output-token ratio, while Qwen3.5-2B, used for the main results, attains the highest final accuracy and mean speedup. Selection quality should be evaluated alongside answer quality and inference cost.

Effect of parallelism.

Parallel chunk processing provides only modest gains because MemDuet must preserve the document order of memory updates. System 1 evaluates chunks concurrently, but System 2 rewrites memory from the first accepted chunk in document order and reevaluates later chunks under the updated memory. As kk increases, more speculative computation may therefore be discarded, and synchronization overhead can outweigh the benefit of concurrency. The best speedup is 1.111×1.111\times at k=8k=8 and 1.75M tokens, whereas k=16k=16 and k=32k=32 slow inference at every evaluated length. Moderate parallelism thus provides the best balance between concurrent evidence discovery and memory consolidation in document order.

Transfer to proprietary models.

MemDuet can be directly applied to proprietary APIs without additional training: a smaller model serves as System 1 to propose candidate chunks, while a stronger model serves as System 2 to accept or reject each proposal before memory rewriting. This plug-and-play setup reduces latency by 70.7–71.8% and cost by 58.2–59.9%, with option accuracy changing by at most 0.60 points.

5 Conclusion

MemDuet combines memory-conditioned parallel evidence selection by a small language model with large-model verification and document-order memory updates. Three-stage training teaches both systems when to update memory and how to consolidate evidence and coordinate decisions. Experiments on three long-context reasoning benchmarks show a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with greater efficiency gains at longer contexts.

Limitations

Our evaluation is limited to three long-context benchmarks and mainly Qwen-family backbones, so generalization to other domains and model families remains uncertain. MemDuet is also less effective on shorter inputs, where selective processing may discard useful evidence; moreover, evidence missed by System 1 cannot be recovered by System 2. Memory updates in document order further limit the practical benefits of parallel execution.

Ethical Considerations

MemDuet studies efficient reasoning over long documents using existing benchmarks and pretrained language models. These resources can contain inaccurate, biased, or sensitive material. Their use and redistribution should respect the applicable licenses and access conditions. Benchmark performance alone does not establish fairness, privacy protection, or suitability for deployment.

Selective processing can omit relevant evidence or minority viewpoints, while repeated memory updates can preserve unsupported claims and discard qualifications. The verifier evaluates memory-update decisions and should not be treated as an independent guarantee of factual correctness. For consequential applications, users should retain access to original documents, inspect supporting evidence, and require human review of outputs. Additional evaluation across languages, domains, and population groups is needed before such use.

Long documents, intermediate memories, and generated answers may expose personal or confidential information. Deployments should minimize sensitive data, restrict access to stored memories and logs, and define appropriate retention and deletion procedures. Users should confirm authorization before transmitting content to proprietary APIs and consider the providers’ data-handling policies.

Lower inference cost may make document analysis more accessible, but can also facilitate large-scale surveillance or unauthorized profiling. Applications should be limited to authorized, legitimate uses. Finally, reduced latency and output-token counts do not directly quantify energy consumption or carbon emissions; environmental benefits require dedicated measurement that also accounts for training and total usage.

Appendix A Experimental Setup

A.1 Dataset Construction

  • •

    RULER-HQA: We combine the RULER evaluation framework (Hsieh et al., 2024), HotpotQA validation questions (Yang et al., 2018), and MemAgent’s controlled-length document construction (Yu et al., 2026). Supporting documents are combined with distractors. The test sets retain the same 128 questions and supporting evidence across length settings, while additional documents increase the input length. Testing covers ten nominal lengths: 7K, 14K, 28K, 56K, 112K, 224K, 448K, 896K, 1.75M, and 3.5M tokens. Documents are divided into consecutive 5,000-token chunks using the updater tokenizer, preserving their order. We reserve the 128 questions in MemAgent’s released development set exclusively for final testing. A separate set of 128 questions from the remaining HotpotQA validation split is used for training-time validation and checkpoint selection (Appendix B.2).

  • •

    LongBench v2: Table 2 uses our four token-length groups, covering all 503 questions. Let LL be the source-context token count measured with the fixed Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct tokenizer: Short (L<32,768L<32{,}768; 116 questions), Medium (32,768≤L<131,07232{,}768\leq L<131{,}072; 188), Long (131,072≤L≤262,144131{,}072\leq L\leq 262{,}144; 100), and Ultra (L>262,144L>262{,}144; 99).

  • •

    2WikiMultihopQA: We use the same evidence-plus-distractor construction strategy as RULER-HQA, following MemAgent (Yu et al., 2026). The data come from FlashRAG (Jin et al., 2025b). We exclude questions missing annotated supporting documents and build a deduplicated title-and-text document pool. Each question retains its reference answers and original context, including all supporting documents. Additional documents are sampled from the pool, excluding that question’s original documents, to reach 100, 400, 1,600, or 6,400 documents. Each context is shuffled and concatenated with numbered document headers. These counts define the nominal 14K, 56K, 224K, and 896K settings in Table 2.

    All lengths and methods share the same 128 questions: the first 128 of 640 sampled eligible question indices.

A.2 Models and Baselines

  • •

    System 1: We use Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and Qwen3.5-2B as small-model backbones (Yang et al., 2025a; Qwen Team, 2026).

  • •

    System 2: We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the large-model backbone (Yang et al., 2025a).

We group the baselines in the complete comparison (Table A4) by their long-context processing mechanism:

  • •

    Base-model approaches: Qwen2.5-Instruct (7B, 14B, and 32B) (Yang et al., 2025a), Qwen2.5-1M (7B and 14B) (Yang et al., 2025b), QwenLong-L1 (32B), and DS-Distill (7B, 14B, and 32B) generate answers directly from the supplied context, without an external retrieval or memory-update workflow.

  • •

    RAG-based approaches: RAG and Search-R1, both using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, retrieve relevant documents before or during answer generation.

  • •

    Agent-based approaches: RL-MemAgent (7B and 14B), InfMem (4B), GRU-Mem (7B), LycheeMemory (7B, −G-G and +G+G), ReMemR1 (7B), and QwenLong-L1.5-30B-A3B (Shen et al., 2025) maintain and update memory to process long contexts incrementally.

A.3 Evaluation Metrics and Protocol

Open-ended question answering.

For RULER-HQA and long-context 2WikiMultihopQA, we report normalized substring exact match (sub-EM). We lowercase predictions and reference answers, remove punctuation and English articles, and collapse whitespace. Following the MemAgent scorer, a nonempty extracted prediction receives 1 if either normalized answer is a substring of the other, and 0 otherwise. We take the maximum score over reference-answer aliases and report the mean as a percentage.

Multiple-choice question answering.

For LongBench v2, we report option accuracy: the percentage of questions whose extracted prediction in {A, B, C, D} exactly matches the reference option. Missing or unparseable option labels score 0. This compares option labels without the open-ended QA normalization or substring-matching rule. The question-and-options prompt and final-answer format are given in Appendix E.5.

Inference time and speedup.

Local per-question latency covers initialization, selection, verification, committed rewrites, and answering, excluding model loading, warm-up, and offline input preparation. Rejected or stale requests may still incur processing cost. Within one length setting and the same question cohort, let TMemAgent,jT_{\mathrm{MemAgent},j} and Tmethod,jT_{\mathrm{method},j} denote the inference time of MemAgent and the evaluated method on question jj. Speedup relative to MemAgent is

Speedup=∑jTMemAgent,j∑jTmethod,j.\operatorname{Speedup}=\frac{\sum_{j}T_{\mathrm{MemAgent},j}}{\sum_{j}T_{\mathrm{method},j}}.

MemAgent has a speedup of 1×1\times; values above 1×1\times indicate faster inference than MemAgent.

Output tokens and reduction.

Output tokens include System 1’s output and System 2’s verification, memory generation, and final-answer output. For the same length setting and question cohort, let OMemAgent,jO_{\mathrm{MemAgent},j} and Omethod,jO_{\mathrm{method},j} denote the respective output-token counts on question jj. The output-token ratio rOr_{O} and percentage reduction relative to MemAgent are

rO\displaystyle r_{O} =∑jOmethod,j∑jOMemAgent,j,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j}O_{\mathrm{method},j}}{\sum_{j}O_{\mathrm{MemAgent},j}},
Reduction(%)\displaystyle\operatorname{Reduction}(\%) =100​(1−rO).\displaystyle=100(1-r_{O}).

MemAgent has rO=1r_{O}=1 and zero reduction; a positive reduction means fewer output tokens than MemAgent.

Appendix B Training and Implementation Details

We train MemDuet on 8 ×\times NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs. For inference, we use 1 ×\times NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPU and process one example at a time (batch size 1).

B.1 Stage I: Memory-Contrastive Supervised Warm-up

Training data.

We use 32,758 HotpotQA training questions (Yang et al., 2018) with complete RL-MemAgent-7B teacher-memory trajectories. We randomly select 500 questions for validation and use the remaining 32,258 questions for training. All chunks and memory pairs from the same question remain in the same split.

Contexts are divided into consecutive 5,000-token chunks with the teacher tokenizer. The first chunk initializes memory and is excluded from action training examples. Gold supporting facts identify evidence chunks, and the teacher updates memory only at these chunks in document order. Each subsequent chunk is paired with the question and the memory before that chunk: evidence chunks yield UPDATE examples, while other chunks yield natural SKIP examples. For every UPDATE example, replacing only the memory with the teacher’s post-update memory yields an additional SKIP example:

(q,c,m)\displaystyle(q,c,m) ⟶Update,\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Update}{}, (14)
(q,c,m′)\displaystyle(q,c,m^{\prime}) ⟶Skip.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Skip}{}.

Changing memory alone changes the target to Skip. The training set contains 195,111 examples: 41,180 UPDATE examples, 112,751 natural SKIP examples, and 41,180 post-update SKIP examples. The validation set contains 2,996 examples: 627 UPDATE examples, 1,742 natural SKIP examples, and 627 post-update SKIP examples.

Configuration.

For Stage I, we train a System 1 LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) with rank r=32r=32, scaling parameter αLoRA=64\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=64, and dropout 0.05. We use the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 10−410^{-4}, a cosine annealing schedule, and a warm-up ratio of 0.03. The effective batch size is 64, the precision is bf16, and the training budget is three epochs. The UPDATE and SKIP class weights are 13 and 1, respectively; the paired-memory hinge loss has margin 1 and weight 0.2. The class-weighted action cross-entropy is normalized by the total target-class weight in each batch.

B.2 Stage II: Optimizing System 2 with a Fixed Selector

B.2.1 Dataset Construction

We use MemAgent’s released long-context HotpotQA data (Yu et al., 2026) for the 32,768 training examples derived from the HotpotQA training split. The 128 questions in MemAgent’s released development set are reserved exclusively for final RULER-HQA testing across context lengths (Appendix A.1). For periodic validation and checkpoint selection, we sample 128 additional questions from the remaining HotpotQA validation split with random seed 42. Their long contexts use the same evidence-plus-distractor construction. The resulting validation set is fixed before training, and test results are not used to select checkpoints. Each example pairs a question qq with its long context DD and reference answer y∗y^{\ast}:

𝒟II={(q,D,y∗)}.\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{II}}=\{(q,D,y^{\ast})\}. (15)

For training, we apply center truncation to each long context and divide it into consecutive 5,000-token chunks in document order, retaining at most eight chunks per question. All chunks of an example share the same question and reference answer.

The offline data contain no reference-memory sequence or fixed candidate indices. System 2 generates initialization and replacement memories online. The frozen selector is reevaluated using each generated memory.

B.2.2 Reward Function

We compute answer rewards using normalized exact matching of boxed answers. For each trajectory, we extract the answer inside the last \boxed{...} field in the final 300 output characters as the prediction. We lowercase the prediction and reference answer aliases and apply formatting normalization. The answer reward is 1 if the prediction exactly matches any normalized reference alias; missing, malformed, or unmatched answers receive 0.

For trajectory gg, let rgansr_{g}^{\mathrm{ans}} denote the binary score of the final answer ygy_{g}. We use this score as the training reward:

Rg=Rtask​(yg,y∗)=rgans.R_{g}=R_{\mathrm{task}}(y_{g},y^{\ast})=r_{g}^{\mathrm{ans}}. (16)

For each question, we sample G=16G=16 complete trajectories and compute standardized group-relative advantages using Eq. (8). Each trajectory’s advantage is shared by its verification commitment events and all generated tokens for System 2 policy optimization.

B.2.3 Training Configuration

For the full configuration, we initialize System 1 from the Stage I Qwen3.5-2B model and freeze the selector throughout Stage II. System 2 is initialized from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and all its parameters are optimized. For KL regularization, the generation reference policy is a frozen copy of this initial Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model. It remains fixed throughout Stage II, while the behavior snapshot θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}} is refreshed each iteration.

Stage II collects complete trajectories under (ϕSFT,θold)(\phi_{\mathrm{SFT}},\theta_{\mathrm{old}}). System 2 initializes memory from the first chunk, and the frozen selector evaluates a four-chunk window under the current memory. System 2 scores the selected candidates; independent acceptance tests follow Eq. (4). Only the first accepted candidate in document order triggers a memory rewrite. Subsequent decisions under the old memory are discarded, and processing resumes after the committed chunk. If no candidate is accepted, memory is unchanged and the cursor advances past the window. After document processing, System 2 generates the final answer from the question and final memory.

We use AdamW to update all System 2 parameters with a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}. The selector uses a four-chunk window. Table A1 summarizes the configuration.

With a training budget of 25 epochs, Stage II minimizes Eq. (9). Clipped policy losses are averaged over ℰg\mathcal{E}_{g} separately within each trajectory. KL terms are averaged only over generated tokens 𝒯g\mathcal{T}_{g}, with β=10−3\beta=10^{-3}; verification commitment events receive no KL penalty. Commitment probabilities follow the controller-induced distribution described after Eq. (10). For nt=|ℐt|>0n_{t}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}|>0, the verification event e=(ver,t)e=(\mathrm{ver},t) records a global chunk index ig,t⋆i_{g,t}^{\star} or 00, conditioned on (q,𝒲g,t,ℐg,t,mg,t)(q,\mathcal{W}_{g,t},\mathcal{I}_{g,t},m_{g,t}). This is one verification event per window, marginalizing outcomes after the earliest accepted candidate. An empty candidate set is deterministic and contributes no verification-policy loss. The verification commitment and ordinary memory-update ratios follow Eqs. (10)–(11). Initialization uses (q,c1,minit,mg,0,<ℓ)(q,c_{1},m_{\mathrm{init}},m_{g,0,<\ell}) to score mg,0,ℓm_{g,0,\ell}, and is included among trainable memory-generation tokens. Final answer generation uses the token-level ratio with conditions (q,mg,fin,yg,<ℓ)(q,m_{g,\mathrm{fin}},y_{g,<\ell}) defined in Stage II; its tokens also contribute to the policy loss and KL regularizer. During replay, we update parameters under the fixed rollout conditions and mask inputs and padding in generation losses. Identical-reward groups have zero policy-advantage contribution, but the KL term remains.

B.3.1 Dataset Construction

For Stage III, we reuse the Stage II dataset in Eq. (15), with 𝒟III=𝒟II\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{III}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{II}}. The training set retains the 32,768 examples, and checkpoint selection uses the same separate 128-question validation set as Stage II. The 128 questions in MemAgent’s released development set remain reserved for final testing. No extra supervised action labels, reference memories, or acceptance-derived correctness labels are introduced. The change is online trajectory generation: both current policies produce the selections, verification outcomes, intermediate memories, and answers.

B.3.2 Reward Function

Both policies reuse the Stage II final-answer reward in Eq. (16). The group-relative advantage follows Eq. (8); a single trajectory’s advantage is assigned to selection, verification, memory-generation, and answer events. Accepting a candidate is not an independent correctness reward, and a Skip decision is not omitted merely because it avoids a large-model generation call.

B.3.3 Training Configuration

For the full configuration, System 1 uses Qwen3.5-2B and continues training the LoRA adapters from the selected Stage I checkpoint. System 2 loads the selected Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct checkpoint from full-parameter Stage II training and adds new LoRA adapters. Both backbones remain frozen; optimization updates only the adapter parameters within ϕ\phi and θ\theta. The two systems use separate AdamW optimizers with independent optimizer states and synchronized behavior snapshots (ϕold,θold)(\phi_{\mathrm{old}},\theta_{\mathrm{old}}). Optimizer and scheduler states are reset at the start of Stage III, while checkpoint weights are retained. Dropout is disabled during both rollout and policy replay. Table A2 summarizes the configuration.

Selection events update only System 1 adapters using the ratio in Eq. (13), with the recorded action ag,t,ia_{g,t,i} and conditions (q,ci,mg,t)(q,c_{i},m_{g,t}). Verification commitments update both systems’ adapters through

ρg,tver=Prϕ,θ⁡(it⋆=ig,t⋆∣q,𝒲g,t,ℐg,t,mg,t)Prϕold,θold⁡(it⋆=ig,t⋆∣q,𝒲g,t,ℐg,t,mg,t),\rho_{g,t}^{\mathrm{ver}}=\frac{\Pr_{\phi,\theta}(i_{t}^{\star}=i_{g,t}^{\star}\mid q,\mathcal{W}_{g,t},\mathcal{I}_{g,t},m_{g,t})}{\Pr_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}},\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(i_{t}^{\star}=i_{g,t}^{\star}\mid q,\mathcal{W}_{g,t},\mathcal{I}_{g,t},m_{g,t})}, (18)

where ig,t⋆i_{g,t}^{\star} is the recorded committed chunk index or 00. The full conditions are the recorded query, window, candidate indices, and memory. The commitment probabilities follow the distribution described after Eq. (10); they retain dependence on both systems through the acceptance ratio. Behavior probabilities are fixed. Candidate sets, chunk indices, action labels, and memory strings are replayed as conditioning data, without regenerating them or differentiating through discrete text. Ordinary memory-update tokens use the System 2 ratio in Eq. (11); initialization and final answer generation use the substitutions and full conditions defined in Stage II. Their policy loss and KL regularizer update only System 2 adapters. The complete trajectory factors follow Eq. (17), with no additional verifier-policy factor.

Let ℰg\mathcal{E}_{g} contain all four event types. The clipped loss averages events within each trajectory, as in Stage II. Generation-only KL retains β=10−3\beta=10^{-3} and the same frozen reference policy as Stage II: a frozen copy of the initial Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model. This reference remains fixed across both RL stages. Selection and verification events receive no KL term. Both adapters’ gradients are computed before either optimizer is stepped, and both rollout policies are synchronized before collecting a fresh group.

B.4 Complete MemDuet Inference

B.5 Training-Free Transfer to Proprietary APIs

Models and API versions.

For DeepSeek, we use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as System 1 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 as System 2. For OpenAI, we use GPT-5.6 Luna as System 1 and GPT-5.6 Sol as System 2. Transfer uses task prompts and workflow control without additional SFT or GRPO.

Differences from the full MemDuet method.

The API adaptation differs primarily in training and acceptance. The full method learns the two systems through the three-stage training in Section 3.3. Here, we instead use off-the-shelf proprietary models with fixed parameters, adapting their roles through task prompts and an external controller rather than additional SFT or GRPO.

In the full method, the UPDATE probabilities of System 1 and System 2 determine the acceptance probability in Eq. 4, followed by independent random acceptance tests. In the API adaptation, we do not request action log-probabilities. Instead, generated k/u labels drive the decisions: System 1’s k skips a chunk, while u forwards it to System 2; System 2’s k rejects the candidate, while u directly accepts it. We therefore replace probability-ratio-based speculative acceptance with text verification, without computing the acceptance ratio or drawing separate acceptance random variables.

Request settings.

All calls to both systems use thinking-disabled mode. The output caps are 8,192 tokens for System 1 and 32,768 for System 2. Contexts are split into 5,000-token chunks, with a four-chunk lookahead and a 1,024-token memory budget.

API prices.

Table A3 lists prices in USD per million tokens. The DeepSeek entries are off-peak rates; peak rates are twice these values.

Appendix D Speculative Acceptance

This section distinguishes the coverage supplied by a high-recall selector from the target-distribution guarantee of speculative decoding.

D.1 Difference from Distribution-Preserving Speculative Decoding

Standard speculative decoding combines acceptance with residual resampling after rejection to preserve the target model’s sampling distribution, regardless of draft quality (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). This is distributional equivalence, not a guarantee that the target answer is correct. MemDuet instead speculates over memory-update actions. A System 1 SKIP bypasses System 2, and a rejected UPDATE does not trigger residual resampling. Thus Eq. (4) alone does not preserve System 2’s standalone action or answer distribution. Write dt,id_{t,i} and vt,iv_{t,i} for the System 1 and System 2 UPDATE probabilities, respectively, at the same (q,ci,mt)(q,c_{i},m_{t}). With sampled proposals, the probability of selecting and accepting a chunk is dt,i​min⁡(1,vt,i/dt,i)=min⁡(dt,i,vt,i)d_{t,i}\min(1,v_{t,i}/d_{t,i})=\min(d_{t,i},v_{t,i}). For dt,i=0.4d_{t,i}=0.4 and vt,i=0.6v_{t,i}=0.6, it is 0.40.4, below the verifier’s standalone UPDATE probability 0.60.6.

D.2 Quantified Coverage under High Recall

On a specified distribution of live, memory-conditioned states, let z=Updatez=\text{Update}{} denote a reference UPDATE label. Define selector recall r=Pr⁡(i∈ℐt∣z=Update)r=\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\mid z=\text{Update}{}) and the mean acceptance probability α¯=𝔼[αt,i∣i∈ℐt,z=Update]\bar{\alpha}=\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t,i}\mid i\in\mathcal{I}_{t},z=\text{Update}{}]. If r≥1−εr\geq 1-\varepsilon and α¯≥1−η\bar{\alpha}\geq 1-\eta, the independent uniform acceptance test gives

Pr⁡(i∈ℐt,ξt,i≤αt,i∣z=Update)\displaystyle\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}_{t},\xi_{t,i}\leq\alpha_{t,i}\mid z=\text{Update}{}) (19)
=r​α¯≥(1−ε)​(1−η).\displaystyle=r\bar{\alpha}\geq(1-\varepsilon)(1-\eta).

A sufficient condition for the acceptance bound is vt,i≥1−ηv_{t,i}\geq 1-\eta on selected reference-positive states: for 0<dt,i≤10<d_{t,i}\leq 1, min⁡(1,vt,i/dt,i)≥vt,i\min(1,v_{t,i}/d_{t,i})\geq v_{t,i}. The verifier cannot recover a candidate omitted by System 1. As a hypothetical example, recall 0.990.99 and mean acceptance 0.990.99 yield reference-positive action coverage 0.98010.9801, not answer accuracy 0.98010.9801.

If these bounds hold conditional on the live prefix at each of at most LL reference-positive decisions per question, a union bound gives

pmiss≤min⁡{1,L⁡(ε+η−ε​η)},p_{\mathrm{miss}}\leq\min\{1,L(\varepsilon+\eta-\varepsilon\eta)\}, (20)

where pmissp_{\mathrm{miss}} is the probability that at least one such decision is skipped or rejected. No independence between decisions is required. With acceptance probability one on positives, this reduces to pmiss≤min⁡{1,L​ε}p_{\mathrm{miss}}\leq\min\{1,L\varepsilon\}. Here, live decisions exclude stale results discarded after an earlier rewrite. A held-out aggregate recall does not by itself establish the required conditional bounds on reached states.

Appendix E Prompt Templates

The following prompts are used in MemDuet’s training and inference, covering candidate selection and verification, memory initialization and updating, and final answer generation. The placeholders {prompt}, {memory}, and {chunk} denote the question, current memory, and input document chunk, respectively.

E.1 Candidate Selection

Use: System 1 inference and memory-conditioned action supervision. Inputs: question, current memory, and one raw chunk. Output: one token, k (SKIP) or u (UPDATE), without a memory draft or explanation. Parallel calls substitute the same committed memory. For before/after supervised pairs, the memory placeholder changes and the target action changes; the task text need not be duplicated.

E.2 Candidate Verification

Use: System 2 verifies whether a selected chunk warrants a memory update before memory generation. Inputs and task text are identical to Appendix E.1, with System 2’s own chat template. Output interface: first-position k/u and both action scores, consumed by the controller in Appendix B.4 for open-weight inference. The proprietary API adaptation instead parses generated k/u labels without action scores, as described in Appendix B.5. There is no separate natural-language accept/reject prompt or small-model memory draft.

E.3 Memory Initialization and Updating

Use: first-chunk initialization and committed rewrites. Inputs: question, raw chunk, and previous memory, initialized with No previous memory. Output: complete replacement memory, not an append-only patch. The local MemAgent full-update baseline shares this template; controller protocol wrappers are not extra model instructions.

E.4 Final Answer Generation

Use: answering after document processing. Inputs: question and final committed memory, without raw documents or discarded candidates. Output: the answer in \boxed{}, as below.

E.5 LongBench v2 Multiple-Choice Prompt

For LongBench v2, the {prompt} placeholder in the preceding templates contains the question, all four options, and the letter-answer instruction shown in the <problem> block below. Candidate selection, verification, and memory updates use this same question text. The final-answer template combines it with the final memory and asks for an option letter in \boxed{}. Option accuracy is defined in Appendix A.3.

Appendix F Case Studies

We present three successful trajectories and one failure. Evidence and memory excerpts below are condensed from recorded states, not verbatim model transcripts. Unshown chunks and intermediate rounds are explicitly omitted. Here dd and vv denote the System 1 and System 2 UPDATE probabilities, respectively; α\alpha is the acceptance probability and ξ\xi is the sampled uniform variate.

F.1 Successful Reasoning and Memory Evolution

The trajectory joins the film–novelist fact in c3c_{3} with the birth-date fact in c5c_{5}. The small model’s output is a chunk-selection action; all displayed memories were generated by System 2. Provisional acceptance and commitment in document order are separate events.

The committed memory distinguishes the town from the borough and the 2001 census from later population estimates. The same c4c_{4} changes from UPDATE to SKIP after that rewrite, directly illustrating memory-conditioned selection and the invalidation of decisions made under an earlier state. This is an observed trajectory, not a counterfactual intervention.

This case shows a different successful path: the necessary evidence is available immediately, and later processing preserves it without further memory generation. The c9c_{9} rejection is a sampled acceptance-rule outcome, not evidence that its text is factually false or necessarily irrelevant. The generation count describes this trajectory; it is not a latency measurement or a general efficiency estimate.

F.2 Failure Analysis

The c6c_{6} rewrite binds the director’s birth date to the novelist; later evidence repairs the name but not the date. This reveals incomplete memory repair. Acceptance does not certify truth, and the trace establishes neither a causal false SKIP nor failure prevalence. The shorter successful case differs in evidence order and distractors, precluding a controlled length comparison.
